Also known as average path length or characteristic path length. Distances are counted in hops (number of edges) with a breadth-first search from every node, so edge weights are ignored. In a directed graph a pair `(u, v)` counts only if `v` can be reached from `u` by following edge directions, and `(u, v)` and `(v, u)` are separate pairs. The cost is one traversal per node, roughly `O(n * (n + m))`. The mean distance is a single-number summary of how compact a network is, and is used for: - testing for small-world structure (short average paths despite local clustering) - comparing how quickly information or contagion can travel in different networks - tracking how a network's reach changes as nodes or edges are removed or added ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [unconnected]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Controls what happens when some pairs of nodes cannot reach each other. If `True` (default), unreachable pairs are simply left out and the result is the average over all reachable pairs, pooled across components. If `False`, the method returns `None` unless every node can reach every other node (for directed graphs, this means the graph must be strongly connected). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Average shortest path length, or `None` if graph is disconnected (when `unconnected=False`). Also `None` for an empty graph or one in which no node can reach any other. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The mean distance $\bar{d} = \dfrac{1}{|R|} \sum_{(u, v) \in R} d(u, v)$ is averaged only over pairs $R$ that are actually reachable, which matters for directed or disconnected graphs. This quantity, also called the *characteristic path length*, is what Watts and Strogatz used to identify small-world structure: real networks tend to display much shorter $\bar{d}$ than a regular lattice of the same size while clustering stays lattice-like. In scale-free graphs, $\bar{d}$ grows only logarithmically with $|V|$, and $\bar{d}$ itself appears in epidemiological estimates of average time-to-infection along a contact network. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a four-node path the six pairs are at distances 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, and 1, so the mean distance is `10 / 6`, about `1.67`: ::: {#4e80ef9a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) graph.mean_distance() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1.6666666666666665 ``` ::: ::: Adding a shortcut from A to D turns the path into a cycle and brings the far ends together, lowering the mean distance to `8 / 6`, about `1.33`: ::: {#01ffaadf .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_edge("A", "D") graph.mean_distance() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1.3333333333333333 ``` ::: ::: For a disconnected graph, the default averages over the pairs that can reach each other. Here the pairs within the chain A-B-C (distances 1, 2, 1) and the pair D-E (distance 1) give `5 / 4 = 1.25`, while `unconnected=False` refuses to answer and returns `None`: ::: {#4e05a244 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} split = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("D", "E")]) ) (split.mean_distance(), split.mean_distance(unconnected=False)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (1.25, None) ``` ::: :::
